4-2-1.title: Neuron structure
4-2-1.explanation: A neuron is a specialised information-processing and information-transmitting cell. Its major structural regions are the soma (cell body), dendrites, axon and terminal buttons. Dendrites generally receive incoming information, the soma maintains the cell and integrates inputs, and the axon carries the neural message toward terminal regions. A key exam distinction is Dendrites and axons have different typical directions of information flow: dendrites receive toward the cell body, whereas the axon carries the neural message away toward terminals. Myelin insulates axons and can increase conduction speed. For exam application, For a structure-function question, map the part to its role: dendrite = receiving, soma = cell body, axon = conducting, terminal = communicating with the next cell. The exam-relevant terms and relationships to retain are axon terminals.

inline_nudges.label: Exam caution
inline_nudges.text: Dendrites and axons have different typical roles.

4-2-3.title: Types of neurons
4-2-3.explanation: Neurons can be distinguished by their role in information flow. Sensory (afferent) neurons carry information toward the central nervous system, motor (efferent) neurons carry commands away from the CNS to effectors, and interneurons connect neural pathways within the CNS. A key exam distinction is Afferent means toward the CNS; efferent means away from the CNS. The distinction is about direction of information flow, not whether a neuron is physically located in the brain or spinal cord. For exam application, If a PYQ asks whether a pathway carries sensory information toward the CNS or motor commands away from it, use the afferent/efferent direction rule first. The exam-relevant terms and relationships to retain are sensory/afferent, motor/efferent.

inline_nudges.label: Exam caution
inline_nudges.text: Afferent/efferent are defined relative to the CNS.

4-2-4.title: Neural impulse
4-2-4.explanation: Neural signalling within an axon depends on changes in membrane potential. At rest the neuron maintains a resting potential; sufficient stimulation reaches threshold and initiates an action potential. Depolarization is followed by repolarization and a refractory phase. A key exam distinction is An action potential is not graded in amplitude: once threshold is reached, the action potential follows an all-or-none pattern. In myelinated axons, saltatory conduction makes the signal appear to jump between nodes of Ranvier. For exam application, When a question asks what happens after threshold, retrieve the sequence: depolarization → repolarization → refractory period.

inline_nudges.label: Exam caution
inline_nudges.text: Stimulus intensity is not coded by larger action potentials.

4-2-5.title: Synaptic transmission
4-2-5.explanation: Communication between neurons occurs across a synapse rather than by direct physical continuity. An action potential reaching the axon terminal triggers processes that allow neurotransmitter substances to be released into the synaptic cleft and influence the receiving cell. A key exam distinction is Neural impulse refers to electrical signalling within the neuron; synaptic transmission concerns communication from one cell to another across the synaptic gap. Do not treat these as identical processes. For exam application, If a stem moves from an action potential at the terminal to release of a chemical messenger and its effect on another cell, the tested concept is synaptic transmission.

inline_nudges.label: Exam caution
inline_nudges.text: A neurotransmitter's effect depends on its receptor/context.
